study_identification.title: Delineating the Heterogeneity of Alzheimer's Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment Using Normative Models of Dynamic Brain Functional Networks

study_characteristics.study_objective: To elucidate the heterogeneity of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) by constructing sex-specific normative age models of dynamic brain functional networks and mapping individual deviations to identify robust subtypes based on dynamic functional connectivity patterns. The study aims to characterize neurophysiological heterogeneity and identify disease subtypes using deviation patterns from normative models.

dataset_name.answer: Cam-CAN (Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Brainnetome Toolkit; slice timing correction; realignment; spatial normalization to MNI space at 2mm×2mm×2mm; regression of nuisance signals (linear trends, six motion parameters, first-order differences, white matter and CSF signals); temporal bandpass filtering (0.01-0.08 Hz); Brainnetome Atlas (246 regions); Yeo-17 network template

quality_checking_detail.answer: Exclusion criteria included: (1) subjects with poor fMRI data quality, subjects without complete demographic information, and subjects without MMSE scores; (2) removal of subjects with large head motion in any direction corresponding to >3 mm or any rotation >3°; (3) matching the age and sex of subjects at each center. Framewise displacement (FD) was monitored across datasets (Dataset 1: 0.24±0.13; Dataset 2: range 0.13±0.06 to 0.30±0.28; Dataset 3: 0.79±0.80).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: To avoid the influence of multiple sites on the calculation of deviations, the mean deviation of the NC participants was computed as a baseline for each site and adjusted the z scores for patients with MCI and AD accordingly. Dataset 2 (MCAD) included data from 7 different 3T MRI scanners. The normative model was trained on single-site data (Dataset 1, Cam-CAN) and then applied to multi-site datasets (Dataset 2 with 7 sites and Dataset 3 ADNI).

software_tool.answer: Not explicitly specified (custom implementation based on Gaussian process regression)

response_variable.answer: Dynamic functional connectivity features: average functional connectivity strength (a-FCS) and fluctuation characteristic of connection strength (f-FCS) for each of 17 Yeo networks (34 features total)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and sex were used as covariates in Gaussian process regression. The study built sex-specific normative age models, indicating sex stratification.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses site effects by computing mean deviation of NC participants as a baseline for each site and adjusting z-scores accordingly. Motion (framewise displacement, FD) was measured and reported across datasets. However, the paper does not provide comprehensive validation of how well the model handles heteroscedasticity, non-linearity beyond what GPR naturally accommodates, or other nuisance structures. The normative model uses GPR which can handle non-linear relationships, but explicit validation of handling various nuisance structures is limited.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To avoid the influence of multiple sites on the calculation of deviations, we computed the mean deviation of the NC participants as a baseline for each site and adjusted the z scores for patients with MCI and AD accordingly. (page 6, Methods section). Gaussian process regression is grounded in a distribution over functions, facilitating Bayesian nonparametric interpolation. This approach ensures robust fitting for nonlinear relationships among variables and delivers consistent estimation of predictive uncertainty. (page 5, Methods section)
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text page 5-6, Methods section on Normative Modeling and Estimation of Individual Deviation Patterns

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study performed 10-fold cross-validation on Dataset 1 (Cam-CAN) before applying the model to Datasets 2 and 3. This represents validation using non-independent data within the same domain (the training dataset).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To assess the generalizability of the model, we used 10-fold cross-validation before applying the model trained on datasets 1 to dataset 2 and dataset 3. The 10-fold cross-validation indicated an overall standardized mean squared error close to 1 (0.960±0.038) and a mean squared log-loss close to 0 (-0.018±0.021) (Figure S1).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text page 5, Methods section on Normative Modeling; Results page 8

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not validate the normative model using an independent healthy control dataset from the same domain. The model was trained on Dataset 1 (Cam-CAN) with 10-fold cross-validation, but no separate independent healthy control dataset from the same domain was used for validation. The model was applied to Datasets 2 and 3, but these are different domains (multi-site clinical datasets) rather than independent same-domain validation data.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Finally, the normative model was trained based on dataset 1 for subsequent disease deviation analyses. (page 5, Methods). The model trained on Dataset 1 was then applied to Dataset 2 (MCAD, multi-site clinical data with patients) and Dataset 3 (ADNI, with MCI patients).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main text page 5, Methods section on Normative Modeling

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The normative model trained on Dataset 1 (Cam-CAN, single-site healthy controls) was applied to and validated on different domain datasets: Dataset 2 (MCAD, 7-site multi-center clinical dataset with AD and MCI patients) and Dataset 3 (ADNI, multi-site longitudinal dataset with MCI patients). The study demonstrated reproducibility across these different domains by showing consistent subtype identification in independent datasets.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: We replicated the experiment on dataset 3 to investigate the robustness of our findings. In dataset 3, the group-level deviation patterns of a-FCS and f-FCS for individuals with MCI were consistent with those in dataset 2 (Figure 5A). The deviation patterns of corresponding subtypes in both datasets exhibited significant positive correlations (Figure S6), which indicated that the deviation patterns obtained from different datasets are robust.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main text page 10-11, Results section on Progression and Cognitive Characteristics of Subtypes

clinical_dataset.answer: Dataset 2: MCAD (Multicenter Alzheimer's Disease Imaging Consortium, 7 sites); Dataset 3: ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative)

clinical_groups_n.answer: Dataset 2: NC:257; MCI:257; AD:295. Dataset 3: NC:259; MCI:184

clinical_groups_age.answer: Dataset 2: NC: 66.9±6.8 years; MCI: 68.6±8.9 years; AD: 68.9±8.3 years. Dataset 3: NC: 71.5±6.0 years; MCI: 72.0±7.8 years

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score calculated as: z = (y - ŷ) / sqrt(σ₁² + σ₂²), where ŷ is the predicted value, y is the observed value, σ₁ is the prediction uncertainty, and σ₂ is the variance from normal distribution. Individual deviation patterns represented by 34 deviation z-scores (17 a-FCS + 17 f-FCS features). Mean deviation of NC participants used as baseline for each site to adjust z-scores.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: K-means clustering (100-repeated procedure) to identify subtypes based on 34 z-scores; Euclidean distance used between participants. Optimal cluster number determined using 28 indices from NbClust package. Stability measured across 100 clustering replicates (average stability >95%). BIRCH clustering used for validation (>80% consistency). Two-sample t-tests with age, sex, and head motion as covariates for group comparisons (FDR correction, α=.05). ANOVA and post-hoc t-tests for clinical characteristics (MMSE, MoCA) with age and sex as covariates. Spearman correlations to assess similarity between subtype deviation patterns. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with logarithmic rank test for MCI-to-AD conversion risk. Linear regression models for cognitive decline trajectories with age and sex as covariates. Confusion matrices to assess robustness across different clustering algorithms and atlases.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two distinct subtypes were identified for both AD and MCI with significant differences in brain functional phenotypes, spatial atrophy patterns, disease progression trajectories, and cognitive decline rates; subtypes with negative deviation patterns (AD-2, MCI-2) showed higher conversion risk and faster cognitive decline.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study identified two subtypes each for AD and MCI based on dynamic functional connectivity deviation patterns. AD-1 (39.3%, n=116) and MCI-1 (43.6%, n=112) exhibited predominantly positive deviation patterns in average functional connectivity strength (a-FCS) and fluctuation (f-FCS), particularly in sensorimotor network (SM), ventral attention network (VAN), default mode network (DMN), and limbic network (LIM). In contrast, AD-2 (60.7%, n=179) and MCI-2 (56.4%, n=145) showed significant negative deviation patterns across all brain regions for both a-FCS and f-FCS, especially in SM, dorsal attention network (DAN), and DMN. High positive correlations were observed between corresponding AD and MCI subtypes (r=0.89, p<.0001 for both AD-1/MCI-1 and AD-2/MCI-2), suggesting shared deviation patterns. Structurally, AD-2 and MCI-2 exhibited reduced gray matter volume (GMV) and cortical thickness in precuneus, cingulate gyrus, and anterior cingulate lobe, while AD-1 and MCI-1 showed increased GMV in these DMN-related regions, potentially indicating compensatory mechanisms. Functional connectivity strength analysis revealed that AD-2 and MCI-2 showed significant decreases across majority of functional networks compared to controls, while AD-1 and MCI-1 exhibited increased FC strength. Clinically, AD-1 had higher MMSE scores than AD-2 (p<.005), though no significant MMSE difference was found between MCI-1 and MCI-2 in Dataset 2. In the longitudinal analysis (Dataset 3, 4-year follow-up), MCI-2 showed higher proportion of conversion to AD and more rapid progression than MCI-1 (p=.028). MCI-2 exhibited significantly poorer baseline scores and more rapid decline in everyday language abilities, memory, and visuospatial abilities compared to MCI-1. The findings were replicated across different atlases (Power-264 and Schaefer-200) with >80% consistency, and consistent deviation patterns were observed across two independent MCI datasets. The normative model showed high robustness with 10-fold cross-validation yielding standardized mean squared error of 0.960±0.038 and mean squared log-loss of -0.018±0.021.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, scanning protocols varied across datasets and sites, though site effects were mitigated by computing mean deviation of NC participants as baseline for each site. Second, longitudinal data were unavailable in the in-house dataset (Dataset 2), requiring validation using ADNI participants with MCI. The sample size of the MCI group with longitudinal data is relatively small, requiring careful interpretation of some results. Third, various neuropathological patterns identified across different imaging modalities may give rise to distinct subtypes, and the extent to which subtyping findings from other features/modalities correspond to overlapping patient subgroups remains unclear.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that normative modeling of dynamic functional connectivity patterns can identify clinically meaningful subtypes of AD and MCI that differ in disease progression and cognitive decline trajectories. The negative deviation subtype (MCI-2) represents a high-risk group for MCI-to-AD conversion with more severe structural atrophy and functional disruption. The findings provide new insights for developing early prevention and personalized treatment strategies for AD. The robustness was demonstrated through multiple approaches: 100-repeated clustering procedure (>95% stability), validation with different clustering algorithms (>80% consistency with BIRCH), replication across different brain atlases, and consistent results across two independent MCI datasets.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is notable for using dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) features rather than static FC, extracting average functional connectivity strength (a-FCS) and fluctuation characteristics (f-FCS) from sliding time window analyses (60-second windows). The normative model was sex-specific and trained on a large single-site dataset (Cam-CAN, n=644) spanning a wide age range (mean 54.8±18.5 years), then applied to multi-site clinical datasets. The study used Brainnetome Atlas (246 regions) parcellated into 17 Yeo networks, resulting in 34 features per individual. Quality control was rigorous with motion thresholds (>3mm translation or >3° rotation) and exclusion of subjects with poor data quality or incomplete demographics. The deviation z-score calculation incorporated both prediction uncertainty (σ₁) and variance from normal distribution (σ₂). Dataset 2 (MCAD) included 7 sites with various 3T scanners (Siemens Trio Tim, Siemens Skyra, GE Signa HDx, Siemens Verio) with different acquisition parameters detailed in Table S2. Dataset 3 (ADNI) included longitudinal follow-up data (4 years) allowing assessment of MCI-to-AD conversion and cognitive decline trajectories. Cognitive assessments included MMSE (all datasets), MoCA (5 sites in Dataset 2, Dataset 3), and Everyday Cognition Scale - Study Partner Report (EcogSP) subscales in Dataset 3 for longitudinal analysis. The study also performed structural MRI analyses using CAT12 toolbox to extract regional gray matter volume and cortical thickness from the Brainnetome Atlas. Replication experiments validated findings across Power-264 Atlas and Schaefer-200 Atlas in addition to the primary Brainnetome Atlas. Statistical analyses controlled for age, sex, and head motion (framewise displacement) as covariates. The paper was received January 5, 2024, revised May 15, 2024, and accepted May 30, 2024.
